speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Income Tax (Amendment) Bill covers 38 amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of these, 13 amendments arose from the Budget Statement in February 2021, as well as COVID-19 support measures announced earlier this year to help workers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another 25 amendments arose from the periodic review of Singapore’s income tax regime.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have sought views from the public on the draft Bill earlier this year and have taken into account the feedback received.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We thank all the contributors for their inputs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 32 of the Bill provides for this amendment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, the scope of the Double Tax Deduction for Internationalisation (DTDi) scheme has been enhanced to cover additional qualifying expenses, for example, specific expenses incurred to participate in approved virtual trade fairs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 8 and 11 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is to help us encourage our firms to internationalise.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, the 250% tax deduction for qualifying donations to Institutions of Public Character (IPCs) has been extended for another two years to Calendar Year (CY) 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, to continue supporting corporate volunteering, the Business and IPC Partnership Scheme (BIPS) has been extended for another two years to CY 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 14 and 29 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We hope this will continue to encourage Singaporeans to give back to the community.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Fourth, mandatory or voluntary monetary support payments that tenants receive from their landlords in 2021 will not be taxed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will allow tenants to benefit from the full amount of the monetary support payments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Landlords will also be allowed to claim income tax deductions for these monetary support payments they made to tenants in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is to facilitate the passing on of rental waivers granted to master tenants of qualifying Government-owned commercial properties to their sub-tenants, as well as the making of monetary support payments by landlords to their tenants in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 7, 16 and 19 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF regularly reviews and refines the income tax regime.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we will set out the tax treatment for two situations: where trading stock is appropriated, or used, for non-trade or capital purposes, and vice versa.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, where capital assets become trading stock.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: IRAS’ current tax treatment of such situations is similar to the practice and case law of the UK.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The proposed amendments will now codify this current tax treatment into our tax legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Trading stock held by taxpayers may be appropriated for non-trade or capital purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, a property developer may decide to stop trying to sell unsold units and instead keep them for long-term capital gains.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In such cases, we will treat the market value of the trading stock on the date of appropriation as income at that juncture.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Any gain, which is arrived at after deducting expenses, will then be subject to tax, while any loss is allowed as a deduction.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This proposed amendment is necessary to protect our revenues.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because without this amendment, there would be revenue loss from deductions claimed by the taxpayer when the asset was held as trading stock, whereas any gain on the subsequent disposal of the asset will be treated as capital in nature and not subject to tax in Singapore because we do not have a capital gains tax.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Conversely, non-trade or capital assets may become trading stock.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, a property developer may choose not to hold its investment property and redevelop it for sale.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When the redeveloped property is subsequently sold, the gains are computed and subject to income tax.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The proposed amendments provide that in computing such gains, the cost of the trading stock is its market value on the date the asset, in this instance the investment property, becomes trading stock.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 3, 20, 21, 27 and 61 of the Bill provide for these amendments that pertain to the clarification of our tax rules for the purposes where trading stock is appropriated for non-trade or capital purposes and vice versa.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, we will facilitate IRAS’ effectiveness when it administers public schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the past two years, we have introduced and enhanced many support measures, like the Jobs Support Scheme and the Jobs Growth Incentive, to help businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: IRAS has stepped up to support this effort by centralising and taking on the business disbursement functions for nine such schemes, which will be added to the Ninth Schedule of the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As part of the quality assurance process to ensure that public schemes are administered as intended, such as disbursing the correct amount of payments to eligible firms, IRAS needs to work with external auditors to check and audit its scheme allotment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This includes checking against income tax data to verify a company’s eligibility for public schemes, for example, whether it is an SME.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Safeguards are provided for in the Bill to ensure the proper usage of such tax data.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, the Comptroller of Income Tax will be able to restrict the extent of information that needs to be made available to the authorised persons.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Authorised persons who are granted access to the protected data will be prohibited from copying or retaining the data, or disclosing the information to other parties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition, to protect data privacy, identifiers will be masked before any data is released to auditors under this provision.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 2 and 57 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Related amendments will be made to the GST Act, Property Tax Act, Stamp Duties Act, Betting and Sweepstake Duties Act, Private Lotteries Act and Estate Duty Act.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 50, 55 to 60 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, several pieces of feedback were accepted and we see their imprint in today’s Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOF will continue this good practice of holding public consultations and accepting productive feedback.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about tax deductions for donations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans should donate to social and community causes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would like to raise questions about one kind of recipient: donor-advised funds (DAFs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To my understanding, donations to DAFs are eligible for income tax deductions if the DAF is designated to offer grants to Institutions of Public Characters (IPCs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: DAFs have become more popular around the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this growth, lawmakers and experts have criticised the rise of DAF-related "zombie philanthropy".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is the trend where DAFs hold on to donations indefinitely and fail to disburse them to charities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The government loses tax income immediately due to tax deductions, while society benefits only belatedly as donations sit untouched for a long time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On this point, I would like to raise three questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can the Minister share what information is typically requested under section 37(3)(b) of the Income Tax Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, what information has it previously requested when an individual attempts to claim tax deductions using donations to a DAF?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, can the Ministry share how the Government proactively guards against the problem where donors claim tax exemptions, tax deductions for donations to DAFs while the DAFs fail to disburse funds to the IPCs in a timely manner?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know DAFs are meant to encourage charitable giving and I have no broad concerns with their existence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there may be room for stronger tax rules on DAFs that tie the incidence of tax deductions with the distribution of the funds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such rules would promote stronger governance of intermediary charity groups and promise more timely benefits for society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point today is about data secrecy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill empowers IRAS to offer people access to highly confidential government data for the purpose of auditing the administration of public schemes, such as of IRAS’ IT systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such people can copy government records for conducting their audits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this amendment may help IRAS undertake vital audits, I am concerned that it may not promise sufficient safeguards for data secrecy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On this, I have two questions on the topic of excess for the Minister’s clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What scenarios fall within and outside the purpose of the audit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be reasonable for a data audit firm to create extensive digital back-ups stored on their own systems?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Government determine whether the backups are excessive in scope?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why do the amendments not penalise permitted people from holding on to copies of government records for excessive amounts of time?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, we agree that even IT auditors should not be holding on to confidential government records for longer than necessary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Copies of government records held in excessive scope for excessive time increase the likelihood and severity of data leaks and data misuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will take strong action to ensure vital government records are used and copied in a responsible way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point today is about tax deductions for landlords.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this COVID-19 crisis, more than before, Singaporeans have learned the immense powers landlords have over commercial tenants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Commercial tenants have gone out of business as they struggle to pay their rent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many groups, such as the Restaurant Association of Singapore and Singapore Tenants United for Fairness, have spoken in chorus about the lack of flexibility from landlords.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has tried our best to urge landlords to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the pleas have often fallen on deaf ears.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a result, in the past year and a half, this House has to pass laws compelling landlords to provide rental waivers, to allow penalty-free termination of rentals and, most recently, to match rental support provided by the Government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems to encourage a somehow perverse situation where a landlord can evict a failed tenant and then pay reduced taxes on their rental income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why should landlords receive financial incentives when they evict a tenant and keep the property vacant?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The outcome is a net loss for society as productive land is left unused.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, how will IRAS ascertain whether a landlord has made "reasonable efforts" to find a new tenant during the vacancy period?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This loosely defined clause appears to be the only check in these amendments against the scenario I have just described.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be important to clarify how IRAS intends to implement it and guard against bad-faith actors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the provisions and exemptions to reduce some of their overheads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, I would like to highlight five issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I am concerned about ensuring adequate revenue streams from the loss of income tax due to the exemptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government has already had to dip into reserves twice to fund the COVID-19 package.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Through the Government’s prudent planning and reallocation of resources, we are assured that we do not need to expect to tap on the reserves anytime soon.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, it is apparent that the costs to deal with the economic effects of the pandemic are rising.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In these trying times, it seems that the Government would continue to fund the bulk of the COVID-19-related healthcare expenses for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With reduced tax revenues, how does the Government ensure that the expenses remain sustainable?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These exemptions should remain sustainable, in case they have to be extended in light of the persistent uncertainty of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Businesses have been accorded a litany of support measures to tap on, from the JSS to rental waivers, training grants and schemes, and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do we really need to further exempt in areas that companies are supposed to strategise and exercise prudence on, as part of running a business?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am referring specifically to packaging, provision of doubtful debts and diminution in value of investments and renovations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, companies that have had to invest in R&R works to pivot their business, or to fulfil safe management requirements owing to the pandemic, should be the intended recipients of this tax exemption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, there are also companies that have clearly expanded and are thriving due to the pandemic: delivery companies and online office solutions come to mind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There must be a way to differentiate between the former and latter type of companies, as the latter are not the intended recipients of these tax exemptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These companies should indeed be applauded but they should be assisted through other schemes and grants that we already have in place which reward companies that are expanding or hiring more employees.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As for tax exemptions on the design of packaging for overseas markets, I understand that this is meant to support internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we should be promoting green and sustainable packaging, in line with the global call for more sustainability efforts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would appear contradictory to our long-term goals of reducing waste in packaging, if companies can get subsidised for extravagant packaging.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not to make things difficult for businesses, but to be judicious in providing rebates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to continue providing the necessary assistance to businesses and workers for as long as needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond tax exemptions, further support can be given in the form of mentorships and consultations, to guide businesses to tap on the existing relevant support schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have spoken about this before in my earlier speeches.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Understandably, the GST hike was announced before the pandemic and there were plans to implement measures to cushion the impact on the lower- and middle-income groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, residents have expressed the sentiment that the GST hike should only be implemented after the job market stabilises, hopefully, in the short to medium term.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so as we brace ourselves for overall increases in the cost of living over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mdm Deputy Speaker, there must be increased vigilance against unscrupulous companies who may manipulate the provisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the past two years, we have seen how some errant employers either tried to make money off the Jobs Support Scheme by falsifying CPF contributions, or asked employees to return part of their monthly wage in cash.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some would also split wages across business entities to circumvent the salary ceiling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the methods of auditing to prevent such acts from happening?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is relevant, especially in reference to clause 7 of section 13ZA, which relates to the exemption of certain payments received, in connection with COVID-19 events.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is consistent with the Cybersecurity Act 2018, as what the Minister has said, and the Regulation of Imports and Exports Regulations (RIER).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This also helps to prevent unscrupulous companies from manipulating the provisions, a point I made earlier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In practice, it is difficult to detect corporate crime like money laundering and fraud.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It does not mean that this does not exist.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have seen recent high profile cases involving Hin Leong and the fraudulent Envy nickel trading scheme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Whistle-blower protection is key to good corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It allows employees who want to do the right thing to speak up, alert the authorities and limit damage before it becomes too late.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, the introduction of whistle-blower protection in tax statutes is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The company may also place pressure on the whistle-blower, for example, by threatening to derail his career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Protection of a whistle-blower’s identity in the context of proceedings is scant reassurance, when they could still be retaliated against in other forms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without further protection, whistle-blowers will still be reluctant to come forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many continue to struggle to stay afloat to provide jobs for Singaporeans and to move our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They should be the target of our support schemes and tax exemptions to help them tide over these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government is also running a tight ship with increased demands and expenses, exacerbated by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to ensure that the assistance offered is, as John Maynard Keynes put it wisely and succinctly, targeted, timely and temporary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What we can also be certain of is that this quote for more than 200 years ago, will often be repeated by politicians, even though taxes most certainly do not affect everyone in the same way.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that Income Tax (Amendment) Bills are introduced to Parliament with sufficient regularity as many of the clauses relate to tax changes made in the Government's annual Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech, I would like to first raise some clarifications relating to specific tax measures and tax changes that are raised in the Bill before moving on to share my thoughts on pertinent tax issues, which I believe ought to be seriously considered as part of Singapore's periodic review of the income tax system.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While donations ought to be made on altruistic grounds, I am also supportive of the enhanced deductibility of donations, given that this will continue to encourage Singaporeans to give back to the community and to provide support for the charity sector.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking back at 2020, when the Government gave all adult Singaporeans regardless of income a one-off Solidarity payout of $600, many decided to donate this payout instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding the giving surge in 2020, the persistency of COVID-19 has presented much challenge to charities this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For most charities, donations are the primary means of funding the good work that they do and it is important for them to ensure both the sufficiency and regularity of the donations that they receive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This does not preclude short-term enhancements in future such as back in the year of assessment 2016, where the tax deduction granted is three times.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, with the 250% tax deduction already in place since YA 2010, making permanent a baseline level of tax deduction for donations gives charities the assurance of this continuing support while encouraging Singaporeans to continue supporting the causes that matter to them in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These will include schemes such as the JSS and Wage Credit Scheme, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And the role of IRAS is to be the main tax administrator to the Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, over time, IRAS has also been called upon to go beyond tax collection and to support the Government in disbursing various support grants to companies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do support and believe in the importance of enabling an independent third party audit of how IRAS has been implementing these support schemes to ensure proper accountability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially in the context of COVID-19 where substantial sums of monies are involved and continue to be disbursed in some of these schemes alongside the complex and ever-changing conditions around them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note in section 6(11)(c) that authorised persons must make and subscribe to a declaration of secrecy in accordance with section 1, "must not disclose or make copies of the records or documents and will be guilty of an offence if otherwise." That being said, my concern is less on the deliberate disclosure of information, but more in the inadvertent leakage of such information through data breaches.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the sensitivity of tax information, any such breaches would be disastrous even if the negligent party was charged subsequently.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the spirit of being prudent with taxpayers' information, is there a consideration to codify the requirement to retain such records or documents only for a specific period of time required to conduct the audit and for such authorised persons to declare that all copies of tax information in their possession have been destroyed thereafter?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe the new section provides for greater certainty in the timing and recognition of the tax base in such cases, given that the market value of trading stock on the date of appropriation for capital purposes is treated as income that is subject to income tax at the juncture and, similarly, where the cost of the trading stock is its market value on the date the capital asset becomes trading stock.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, in the context of COVID-19, companies facing economic challenges and cash flow issues may have no choice but to scale down their operations, and in so doing, dispose of their capital goods such as property, plant and equipment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And how would the distinction be drawn between a manufacturer selling off its factory or production line compared to a residential developer which converts its existing office building, formerly held as an investment property to strata units which are on-sold to investors?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, I note under section 10(1)(g) of the Income Tax Act, a so-called "catch-all" provision that taxes any gains or profits of an income nature not falling within paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) under the preceding paragraphs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How would section 10(1)(g) factor into IRAS' consideration as to the factors used to determine whether or not such gains from the sale of what is now deemed to be trading stock are revenue in nature?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First of which is the need to consider implementing a wealth tax in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as COVID-19 ravages across the world, disrupting livelihoods and causing economic hardship to workers and businesses alike, rising equity markets and government stimulus mean that global wealth and the number of high net worth individuals continue to reach record highs globally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure that Members in this House will agree with me that widening wealth inequalities are undesirable over the longer term insofar that they risk leading to tensions that impact our societal cohesiveness.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The idea is not new, of course, and such taxes have been raised by the Workers' Party in this House.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During the Budget debates earlier this year, Deputy Prime Minister Heng agreed that there is scope to further review our wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if this is currently being actively studied by MOF and if so, what is the status of the study?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At a lecture at the Institute of Policy Studies in July, the Managing Director of MAS, Mr Ravi Menon, noted that to address the risk of growing wealth inequality, it made sense to shift the balance in Singapore's tax structure away from taxing income towards taxing wealth, wherein property would form a major component in the Singapore context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, in Singapore, where housing prices have broadly grown in tandem with the economy, high home ownership rates and public housing subsidies have in the past helped to narrow the disparity in household wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But these mitigating factors can only go so far.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An area that I am particularly concerned with is the divergence in public and private home prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Put in other words, household wealth from property is increasingly skewed towards the top 10% to 20% of resident households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If left unchecked, this could lead to greater disparity in inter- and intra-generational wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While well-intended, the fear of further "one-offs" could negatively impact faith in regulatory certainty in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather, in principle, wealth taxes need to be recurring yet sustainable, reasonably easy to implement and hard for the wealthy to avoid so that the middle class does not end up bearing more of the burden.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have used this value just as a starting point for discussion, so as to not penalise the majority of Singaporeans, especially the aspiring middle class.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As home valuations are well documented in Singapore, this will help with policy implementation before we consider wealth taxes on net worth, which more comprehensively captures the wealth of the ultra-wealthy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This also means that for the vast majority of Singaporeans who reside in HDB flats, there will be no wealth tax applied to them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The imposition of such a tax could generate legitimate concerns, one of which pertains to Singapore's status as a financial centre and wealth management hub.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, one also has to bear in mind that Switzerland, as a key financial centre and wealth management hub globally today, is one of the countries that actually has a net wealth tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us also remember that not only does Singapore not have a wealth tax, there is no capital gains tax, no tax on dividends, no inheritance tax, no estate duties, and has one of the lowest effective personal income tax rates globally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, there could be implementation challenges and a wealth tax will take many forms, be it net wealth tax like Switzerland, a property gains tax or an inheritance tax, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, yes, having a wealth tax alone will not eliminate widening wealth inequality in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But do we truly want to have a tax system where our low- to middle-income workers pay more in income tax than a trust fund baby living off his grandparents' inheritance?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second issue is to raise the level of progressivity in our corporate income tax regime to better support our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do recognise that there are features in our current corporate taxes that better benefit SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Corporate income tax rebates being capped at a dollar amount, $15,000 for the Year of Assessment (YA) 2020, for example, would mean large multinational companies (MNCs) would not disproportionately benefit from the corporate income tax rebate of 25% that was given.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2018, Hong Kong implemented the two-tiered profits tax regime to relieve the tax burden for SMEs, in particular.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, we do have the tax exemption scheme for new startup companies and partial tax exemption for all companies which have a similar effect.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, it was in the same year in Budget 2018 that the Government announced tighter restrictions around these schemes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as other support for companies to build capabilities is being strengthened, I hope the Government will consider providing greater tax relief to our SMEs, such as by raising tax exemption limits which are geared towards SMEs, given the challenging domestic trading conditions brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I shared in my speech in July this year, SMEs accounted for 9% of total profit before tax in YA2019, yet, they contributed an outsized 29% of corporate income tax paid.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, similarly, the conclusion can still be made that SMEs collectively paid more tax per dollar of either pre-tax profits or changeable income, as compared to non-SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, what companies report in their financial statements to shareholders are accounting profits, which are audited in Singapore based on the Singapore Financial Reporting Standards, which are, of course, modelled after the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The use of accounting profits as a meaningful basis of comparison on tax rates is made all the more relevant, given the fact that Pillar Two of the G20/OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0 proposal is quite simply using financial accounting income for the determination of the tax base, with a small number of adjustments allowed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my third point in that in the fullness of time, I do hope that the Government will continue to safeguard its taxing rights and view the global minimum tax reforms as an opportunity rather than a threat, given Singapore's strong non-tax advantages and attractiveness to MNCs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Tax receipts which can then be used to reinvest in our people and our local companies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, Mdm Deputy Speaker, notwithstanding my clarifications on the Bill, I support the amendments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our tax policy sends a strong signal of the kind of growth we want to pursue and the kind of society we want to build.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the face of rising inequality and the economic and social disparities that are brought to the fore by COVID-19 globally, we have a moral imperative to enhance progressivity in our tax system and ensure that any tax changes we propose bring us closer towards achieving quality growth and an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, income tax is one of the main sources of our national revenue.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An appropriate tax regime would enable revenue to be fully utilised and promote economic growth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to giving the Government the capacity to regulate macro-policies, it would also promote the development of specific areas.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill are broadly in line with these objectives, especially in this challenging economic environment, to help our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 has led to a widening wealth gap between rich and poor in many countries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order to avoid the rich getting richer while the poor getting poorer in our country, the Government has been improving the situation through a number of inter-Ministry policies and measures, including tax deductions and encouraging individuals and businesses to do more good and to donate to Institutions of Public Character (IPCs).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support and recommend that MOF consider giving higher tax deductions on large donations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe this will help build a more united and caring society.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A good tax regime is one that works towards an ideal society where the needs of all Singaporeans are met.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I would like to comment and ask some questions on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, allow me to comment on the various amendments by section.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Amendment of section 6: regarding the proposal to allow authorised persons access to IRAS records and/or documents containing taxpayers' income information, would the Ministry share specific examples where IRAS' records will be shared with a private sector auditor?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the online exposure attracts a great deal of interest and the companies benefit from many business leads derived from the virtual fairs, can the follow-up marketing and business development expenses be eligible too?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Amendment of section 14ZA: to promote rated retail bond issuances, the amendments seek to extend and refine the Double Tax Deduction (DTD) Scheme for allowing qualifying upfront costs attributable to these bonds.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Based on the current business environment which seems volatile till the first half of 2022, would the Ministry consider extending the option to FY2022 as well?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would be helpful as we are encouraging business owners to automate in order to reduce reliance on foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, for donations of $5 million and $10 million, the tax deductions can go up to 300% and 400% respectively.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will encourage the wealthier members of the community to factor in donations as part of their estate planning.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My concern is that our wealth gap here may widen substantially after this COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of our Institutions of Public Character (IPCs) are doing a great job helping vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope richer Singaporeans can be incentivised to contribute more to support good causes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Amendment of section 104A: regarding the inclusion of a provision to protect informers, how would MOF prevent people with malicious intent from falsifying claims against their competitors or rivals?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With informers so well-protected, genuine or not, how can falsely accused persons or companies defend and protect themselves against fabricated charges?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While this Bill is mainly to effect the extension of measures announced at the Budget this year and the various COVID-19 support measures that we have also announced earlier this year, Members have raised other suggestions and broader concerns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I will respond to these in turn.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should clarify that the Bill gives effect to the implementation of measures that have been announced in the Budget and in the various COVID-19 support packages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They really detail the implementation of measures that have been announced.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Mr Yip had questioned if these exemptions were too generous.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But to clarify, these are not new measures, they were announced earlier either in the Budget or in earlier statements and we are implementing them, and you would see that in the implementation of these measures, we have been quite careful in scoping them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, basically, we are allowing the option to claim tax deductions on an accelerated schedule which provides cash flow support to businesses during this period, but we have not changed the overall caps.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip also asked about tax deductions on provisions of doubtful debts and the diminution of value of investments under section 14I of the Income Tax Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is only available for banks and qualifying finance companies, and is subjected to caps to safeguard against excessive provisions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This existing tax deduction aims to promote the overall soundness and stability of our financial system by catering for the building up of adequate provisions to cushion against potential losses in the financial institutions’ loan and investment portfolios.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The change, which is to be incorporated into this Bill, expands the scope to include specified loans and securities in line with financial reporting standards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Again, there is no change of the prevailing caps in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip was also concerned about tax exemption for packaging costs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I wish to clarify that packaging costs, like any business expense incurred in the production of income, can only enjoy 100% tax deduction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There were also some questions on the Double Tax Deduction for Internationalisation, or DTDi scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That covers, amongst others, specified expenses incurred in the design of packaging for overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These expenses are design costs, not packaging costs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Such design costs include, for example, costs of third-party consultancy fees to design packaging for overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As part of the Budget 2021 measure, we have announced that design costs would be added to the existing list of automatic qualifying expenses under the DTDi scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Don Wee had asked about qualifying expenses in relation to virtual trade fair that qualify for this scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Expenses incurred by firms on overseas advertisement and promotional campaigns on social media, including the engagement of influencers, are covered under the DTDi scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this Bill, we will enhance the scope of the DTDi scheme to cover specified expenses incurred to participate in approved virtual trade fairs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These specified expenses include third-party costs for the design and production of digital collaterals and promotion materials for the approved virtual trade fair, and logistics costs incurred to send samples overseas to potential clients met at the approved virtual trade fair, subject to conditions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, as you can see, we are talking about expanding the scope of qualifying expenses but we have continued to keep a cap on the overall amount at $150,000.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Wee asked if the double tax deduction, or DTD scheme for qualifying upfront cost attributable to retail bonds issued under MAS’ Bond Seasoning and Exempt Bond Issuer Frameworks can be extended to green bonds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Green bonds which meet the qualifying criteria for the DTD scheme can qualify under the scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are to address all the comments about Budget measures, COVID-19 measures which had been announced, but we are talking about the implementation and we want to assure Members that in working out the implementation details as reflected in the amendments in this Bill, we have been careful to make sure that the schemes are carefully and properly designed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Don Wee then also asked about the further extensions of some of the schemes, beyond what had been announced.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, he asked if the option to accelerate the write-off of the cost of acquiring plant and machinery can be further extended for another year, in view of the current situation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should say that each time we ask for additional requests for help for businesses or individuals, we should look at schemes in totality.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not just one particular scheme but we have other schemes in place overall to encourage businesses to invest in new and emerging technologies to sharpen their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We continue to monitor the situation closely and review all our schemes, as needed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Should there be a need to extend any measure, any such extension will then be announced at Budget 2022 and then it will be effected in next year’s Income Tax (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me address the specific comments raised on other amendments outside of Budget and COVID-19 support measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, Mr Louis Chua asked about the new section 10P.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is a scenario where trading stock is appropriated for capital purposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I must clarify first that this is an existing treatment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this is to codify the existing treatment, which is also similar to what is done in Hong Kong and the UK.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Chua asked about the disposal of property, plant and equipment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is not considered as business trading stock in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there would be no appropriation of trading stock and section 10P does not apply under such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the new section 14ZH in the concerns that it may inadvertently reward a landlord who evicts a failed tenant and keeps the property vacant.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This section is in line, again, with the existing tax treatment that IRAS applies up to now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The legislative clarification provides tax certainty for the taxpayers, namely landlords who are taxable on their rental income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, under this section, as long as the landlord demonstrates with supporting evidence that he has made reasonable efforts to secure a tenant during the vacancy period, IRAS will allow tax deduction for qualifying expenses such as property tax, repair, insurance and maintenance of the property incurred during the vacancy period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, what does the landlord have to demonstrate in order to show reasonable effort?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, IRAS would request a taxpayer to provide supporting evidence such as documents showing that the repair was made to the property to keep it in lettable condition; or that a property agent was appointed to find a tenant; or that the property had been advertised for rent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if IRAS is satisfied that reasonable efforts have been made to seek a tenant during the vacancy period, then this section will apply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if IRAS is not satisfied that reasonable efforts have been made to secure a tenant, then the tax deductions will not be allowed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me address the points raised by Mr Ng with regard to donor-advised funds (DAFs).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ng asked for data on the amount of income tax deductions linked with donations to DAFs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not track this data specifically because tax-deductible donations are currently tracked based on IPC and approved grant-maker status, and this is in line with requirements for the receipt of tax-deductible donations under the Charities Act and the Income Tax Act respectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I understand Mr Ng's concerns over ensuring the timely disbursement of funds by DAFs to IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, for DAFs which are themselves IPCs, they have flexibility to disburse the funds for the charitable programmes, no different from other IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think Mr Ng is more concerned about DAFs which are approved grant-makers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, Mr Ng can be assured that we do not have this scenario where donations are being made to grant-makers, but they hold back on disbursing grants to the charities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ng also asked about the information requested by IRAS when an individual attempts to claim tax deductions on their donations to a DAF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Again, IRAS does not separately request for information on tax-deductible donations to a DAF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If the DAF is an IPC or an approved grant-maker, the same reporting requirements applicable to IPCs and approved grant-makers would then apply respectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Wee's suggestion to provide 300% or 400% tax deductions will also result in more tax revenue forgone.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And Mr Louis Chua, likewise, had suggested to make permanent this tax deduction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Again, I appreciate the intent of Mr Louis Chua and Mr Don Wee to promote philanthropy and charitable giving.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have to consider the merits and trade-offs carefully, bearing in mind that we currently have one of the highest tax deduction rates for donations in the world and we want to make sure that any scheme we have in place is fiscally sustainable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In addition, besides tax deduction, the Government also adopts a multi-faceted approach to encourage charitable giving within the community.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us not just look at tax alone.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us look at what we do with regard to non-tax measures as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will continue to review both the tax and non-tax measures to do more for charitable giving.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, several Members asked about data confidentiality issues regarding audits on the administration of public schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In my speech, I mentioned that safeguards are provided for in the Bill to minimise the risk of unauthorised disclosures and the misuse of tax data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, annual revenue data would be provided to auditors to determine the eligibility of SMEs for the Rental Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As revenue size is not part of the scheme design for the Jobs Growth Incentive, such data will not be shared with auditors for the Jobs Growth Incentive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the Comptroller of Income Tax will have the discretion to decide on the extent of information that needs to be made available, subject to the safeguards that I have explained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Various methods like tokenisation would be used to prevent the disclosure of individual data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Authorised persons who are granted access to protected data will be prevented from retaining or making copies of the data provided in the first place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In other words, they can only access data on IRAS-issued devices and only within IRAS' premises.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is no issue of external auditors storing data for excessive amounts of time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Appointed audit firms will also be required to adhere to contractual terms on data confidentiality and ensure that the use of confidential information is only for authorised purposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the event of a breach, the appointed firm will be liable to legal actions under the terms of the appointment contract and penalties under our Acts governing the data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, Mr Yip asked about the methods of audits on the disbursement of schemes like the JSS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS, as the administrator of the JSS, had instituted a robust anti-gaming framework, making use of data from multiple sources to identify and detect abuse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While we are unable to share the specifics of IRAS' anti-gaming operations for good reasons – if you tell people what we are doing, I think it will encourage more gaming behaviour – this framework has been in place since the first JSS payout in April 2020.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For cases suspected of higher fraud risks, IRAS requires the firms to authenticate their CPF contributions before the payouts are released.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Cases with strong corroborative evidence to suggest abuse are reported to the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD) for further investigation and prosecution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I also thank Mr Yip for his support for the introduction of the Protection of Informers, or POI, provision in the Income Tax and other tax Acts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yip asked about whistle-blower protection in other statutes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, the proposed POI provision in this Bill is modelled after similar provisions in the Customs Act and the Cybersecurity Act 2018.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The legislative amendment to better protect informers will also apply to other tax Acts, beside the ITA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Wee asked how we will prevent people with malicious intent from falsifying claims against their rivals or competitors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will carefully examine not only the information provided by an informer, but also other information available to IRAS, and assess the validity of any allegations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will only commence an investigation when it assesses that a prima facie case exists for tax evasion and if the information provided by the informer proves to be reliable and accurate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Apart from IRAS' internal process, the POI provision includes a legislated safeguard, similar to the POI provisions in other domestic legislation, which will mitigate against the risk of informers making false claims.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Chua mentioned wealth taxes and more reliefs and help for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say, in terms of direction, what Mr Louis Chua has suggested is completely aligned with MOF's thinking.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want to address wealth inequalities and we want to do more to support our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in terms of policy intent, we are completely aligned.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But to address wealth inequalities, what exactly do we do?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What sort of measures do we put in place?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is something that we will have to study carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, we already have a form of wealth tax by way of the tax levied on private residential properties today which is tiered according to annual value (AV).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we already have that structure in place in our property tax system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am unable to reveal what we are thinking about now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that will be premature and I do not want to pre-empt the Budget next year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, obviously, we are continuing to consider all options to address, as I have said, number one, income and wealth inequalities; and number two, what more we can do to support SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where SMEs are concerned, I think the data is very clear.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is useful to bear in mind when you look at the data, it is not a homogenous group; it is very diverse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, therefore, if you look at averages or you look at effective tax rates, one can get a misleading picture.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also need to be careful when we look at reliefs and exemptions for SMEs that we do not want to have inadvertent consequence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This discourages them from growing because if they stay small, they pay less tax, I think that will be unhelpful for our SMEs to scale up and grow and develop to become global champions in their own right.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we need to find the right incentives to support them but, at the same time, encourage them to scale up and grow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is something that MOF, together with our economic agencies, continue to study carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will look not only at tax measures but also at non-tax measures, in other words, the kinds of support schemes we can provide to them through grants, loans and equity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, Mr Yip also highlighted the caution that we need to ensure that we spend in a fiscally sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And he is absolutely right because beyond our short-term fiscal response to COVID-19, we are mindful of our long-term fiscal responsibility to maintain a balanced and sustainable Budget position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our prolonged fight against COVID-19 has been facilitated greatly by our ability to tap on Past Reserves for extraordinary measures to protect lives and to safeguard livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But beyond these emergency conditions, when it comes to recurrent expenditure, ongoing expenditure, I think it is very important that we maintain the principle to fund them through recurrent revenues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, it is never easy to implement a tax increase, let alone a GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the end of the day, we must have the courage to make the difficult decisions that are necessary to uphold a culture of fiscal stewardship and fiscal responsibility.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is how we can best serve the interests of Singaporeans, both in the current as well as in the future generations.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.55 pm until 4.15 pm.
